newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Waning mark to flatten European curves.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Waning mark to flatten European curves.

text.p: The ailing mark has created a new window of opportunity for European spread plays as analysts said on Friday they expect further flattening of yield curves.

A Bundesbank rate hike to prop up the crippled mark against the dollar would trigger a sell-off across the short end of Europe, although bargain hunters should soon pile into Italy, bond strategists said.

"If markets sell off uniformally at the short end, then you should be able to find buying opportunities because some markets are much less likely than others to have to follow the Bundesbank," said Sonja Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International in London.

The German mark was slashed to a 7-1/2 year low this week, falling prey to market speculation about a broad European currency union. On Friday, it hit a fresh low of 1.8570 to the dollar after stronger-than-expected July non-farm payrolls.

Dealers are on tenterhooks as the Bundesbank fixed its last repurchase tender for two weeks instead of the usual four, throwing up the possibility the German central bank could use variable-rate tenders to nudge its repo rate up from 3.0 percent.
David Theobald, head of fixed income research at J.P. Morgan in London, said the speed of the depreciation, rather than the level, would trigger a Buba move.
"Our best guess is that weakness will move more gradually than we've seen. By the end of the year, we are calling the mark at 1.90," Theobald said.
A slump to that level in the next four weeks however would be a ticket for a rate rise, flattening the German yield curve with repurcussions throughout the European bond markets.
Theobald said rate hike expectations could also flatten the curves from the long end, although such plays would likely unwind after a rate move.
"Up to the point in which a rate hike happens the market would think it would be a positive thing in a rather perverse fashion, and you get flattening of the curve," he said.
Nomura's Gibbs said aside from Germany, a rate rise would hammer short term debt in the Netherlands, Denmark, Spain and Sweden where central banks are likely to move in tandem with the Bundesbank.
She said the T-note/Bund spread could narrow sharply from around 60 basis points now.
"If the market gets into its head that the Bundesbank is starting on a round of fairly rapid moves, then Italy will also become very vulnerable," she said.
A knee-jerk reaction in Italy, France and Belgium however should soon falter as these economies, struggling with dismal growth rates, hardly warrant a rate rise, she said.

If the Bundesbank pulled the trigger, European bond convergence would happen at a higher level, hence fewer cuts would be expected from the Bank of Italy before Euroepan Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said.
"It implies that the Bank of Italy should be more cautious in easing rates," said Riccardo Barbieri, senior economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
In any event, a series of Italian rate cuts would not kick off before October or November, he said.
But Nomura's Gibbs said any flattening in Italy and France should be tapped.
"There will be an overreaction, and that could be something to exploit," Gibbs said.
But if the Bundesbank stayed on hold and allowed the mark to slide, the long end of European curves would be in trouble, economists said.
"The short end can take a little comfort from a postponement to a stay of execution, but the long end is going to start to worry," said Gibbs.
